summary: This weekly sync reviewed pilot metrics for Orion Atlas' cohort-based prompt reuse experiment and discussed eviction policy tuning to improve KV/prefix cache hit rates during burst windows. Redwood SE presented a set of candidate eviction strategies (rolling TTL, cohort-weighted LRU, session affinity fallback) and a proposed test plan for a 48-hour synthetic surge to validate cost/latency tradeoffs. Customer asked for concrete config examples, and team agreed on next steps including an eviction-policy draft, representative prompt cohorts, and a performance deep dive next week.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-27 10:30 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Jimenez (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Orion Atlas - Head of ML), Danielle Brooks (Orion Atlas - Infra), Tom Nguyen (Orion Atlas - PM)
---
[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick check on time we have about 55, 58 minutes, is that right for folks?
[00:10] Priya Shah: yep that works for us, we have Tom and Danielle here too, Priya on my side.
[00:15] Carlos Jimenez: cool, i'll share my screen in a sec, got the recent dashboard up — the run from last night plus the 6x burst window test.
[00:22] Tom Nguyen: quick note, the product team saw a couple of UX hiccups when cache misses happened during the demo yesterday — those are the things we want to avoid in production.
[00:30] Maya Patel: right, so goal today — review hit rates by cohort, discuss eviction policy adjustments, and agree on the 48-hour surge validation.
[00:38] Danielle Brooks: also want to confirm the VPC peering window for the stress test, we can enable it for a 3hr window or open a broader window if needed.
[00:45] Carlos Jimenez: OK diving in — slide one, overall KV hit rate improved from 27% to 44% after the prompt-signature hashing change, but prefex cache hit is lower for Cohort C. note: transcription sometimes shows prefix as "prefex" in the logs but that's just my slide typos.
[01:02] Priya Shah: where's Cohort C? that's our long-form summarization queries, high token counts, many tokens not reused.
[01:08] Carlos Jimenez: correct, Cohort C tends to have large context windows and fewer exact prefix matches, so the prefix-based reuse gives limited wins there. However KV-level reuse still saves tokens when the generation re-enters an earlier sub-dialog.
[01:22] Tom Nguyen: is that because of how we compute prompt signatures? we hashed full prompt text, right?
[01:28] Carlos Jimenez: currently yes — full prompt hash with normalization. we proposed moving to a cohort-specific signature that normalizes stop sequences and strips ephemeral metadata — that boosted Cohort A/B matches.
[01:40] Priya Shah: can you explain cohort-specific signature quickly, i.e., what changes for our prompts?
[01:46] Carlos Jimenez: sure: for Cohort C we'd keep sentence order and topical anchors but drop session timestamps and request IDs. for chat-like cohorts we'd keep recent N turns, for single-turn summarization we truncate to the first 512 chars before hashing — reduces false negatives.
[02:02] Danielle Brooks: one concern is hash collisions across cohorts causing wrong KV hits — do we namespace the cache?
[02:08] Carlos Jimenez: yes, recommended to namespace by cohort id + model+quantization tag, that avoids cross-cohort pollution.
[02:14] Maya Patel: noted. next — eviction policy. we tested default LRU, rolling TTL 30s, and a hybrid cohort-weighted LRU. Carlos, can you summarize the tradeoffs?
[02:25] Carlos Jimenez: LRU is simple but punishes hot-spiking cohorts during bursts; rolling TTL reduces churn for items that are frequently re-requested within TTL but can hold onto stale entries and increase memory footprint; cohort-weighted LRU keeps entries for cohorts we expect sticky, like interactive chat, while evicting low-value summarization entries more aggressively. the hybrid had the best token-savings during normal traffic but under extreme surge we saw a 12% p99 latency bump because the cache footprint grew and pushed batching efficiency down.
[02:55] Priya Shah: that p99 increase is worrisome — what caused batching efficiency to drop?
[03:01] Carlos Jimenez: during the surge the cache hit rate for the heavy cohort increased, which is good for token cost, but it also increased variance in sequence lengths and KV lookup times, which reduced our ability to pack tokens into consistently shaped batches on the GPU, so the runtime had to fall back to smaller batch sizes.
[03:20] Tom Nguyen: so there's a tradeoff: better token-savings vs throughput and latency SLOs. we prefer predictable p99s over marginal token savings.
[03:27] Maya Patel: totally get that — Redwood's recommendation is to prioritize latency SLOs for now. we can design an eviction policy that tiers cohorts and applies conservative TTLs for the high-latency-sensitive flows.
[03:38] Danielle Brooks: can you show an example config? we need something we can drop into the pilot cluster.
[03:42] Carlos Jimenez: yes, i'll attach some example configs after the meeting. example: cohort-chat: weight 1.0 TTL 45s, cohort-summarize: weight 0.3 TTL 12s, global-max-items 250k, namespace per service. note: this is a high-level example.
[04:00] Priya Shah: curious about session-affinity fallback — can we keep a lightweight mapping so active sessions get preferential reuse?
[04:07] Carlos Jimenez: session-affinity is doable: a small sticky table that points session id to recent KV keys, TTL 60s. it's cheap and avoids cold starts for ongoing sessions, but it must be bounded to avoid memory blowup.
[04:20] Tom Nguyen: what's the memory delta for session-affinity? rough numbers?
[04:24] Carlos Jimenez: we tested a 100k session table with entries of ~160 bytes -> ~16MB, very modest. the bigger cost is the tracking overhead in the runtime but it's within our current Dedicated pool.
[04:35] Priya Shah: interesting. for Cohort C with long contexts, would session-affinity help?
[04:40] Carlos Jimenez: yes, if your workflow has repeated edits in the same user session. but for one-off long-form summarization the benefit is small.
[04:47] Maya Patel: moving on, we ran a 6x burst window last night for 30 minutes. Carlos, show the anomaly chart.
[04:53] Carlos Jimenez: uploads slide — during the 30-min surge, KV hit rose from 44% to 72% for Cohort A, global latency 95th jumped from 210ms to 520ms for some requests. the generator's batching efficiency dropped by 35%.
[05:12] Danielle Brooks: did the runtime fall back to a cheaper model variant at any point? we configured automatic fallback for burst, right?
[05:18] Carlos Jimenez: no model fallback triggered — the routing stayed on the same model. we did see more frequent GC cycles in the runtime due to cache pressure which contributed to latency spikes.
[05:28] Tom Nguyen: GC cycles — is that the runtime's memory management or our infra-level GC?
[05:31] Carlos Jimenez: runtime-level memory reclamation for pre-allocated KV segments. we're planning to tune reclaim thresholds to avoid synchronous pauses.
[05:39] Priya Shah: any quick wins we can apply before the 48-hour test? small changes we can make now?
[05:44] Carlos Jimenez: yes — set cohort TTLs to conservative values (chat 45s, summarize 10s), enable session-affinity for interactive cohorts, and lower global-max-items limit to reduce GC pressure. those should reduce p99 spikes.
[05:58] Maya Patel: action: we'll send the eviction-policy draft and a config diff you can drop into the pilot cluster.
[06:03] Tom Nguyen: great. on evaluation — how are we measuring 'success' for this pilot? token-savings is one metric, but product impact matters more.
[06:11] Priya Shah: for us success = <2% product-visible error rate during bursts, p99 under 350ms for interactive flows, and >30% token savings for steady-state for cohort A/B.
[06:24] Carlos Jimenez: understood — we'll run synthetic tests and present a dashboard with p50/p95/p99, batch shapes, token-savings, and memory metrics.
[06:33] Danielle Brooks: regarding logs — will we get raw KV hit logs or aggregated metrics? we need raw to cross-check.
[06:38] Carlos Jimenez: we'll provide both — raw event logs (redacted) and aggregated dashboards. privacy note: we'll redact user identifiers before sharing.
[06:46] Maya Patel: ok next item — prompt normalization rules. Priya you mentioned you'd share cohorts, can you confirm how many distinct signature rules you want?
[06:55] Priya Shah: we can start with three: interactive chat, short Q/A, long-form summarization. each needs its own normalization.
[07:03] Carlos Jimenez: perfect. normalization examples: chat -> keep last 6 turns, strip ephemeral headers; Q/A -> normalize whitespace & punctuation; summarization -> seed first 512 characters then hash.
[07:15] Tom Nguyen: curious if normalizing will reduce accuracy for hallucination-sensitive prompts.
[07:20] Carlos Jimenez: a valid concern — normalization can mask context, so we'll make it opt-in per cohort and include a rollback flag.
[07:28] Priya Shah: okay that sounds safe.
[07:32] Danielle Brooks: one more infra ask: during the surge test can Redwood throttle client-side retry patterns? some of our clients retry too aggressively on timeouts which worsens cascade effects.
[07:41] Maya Patel: yes, we can propose client-side backoff recommendations and also apply server-side rate smoothing to reduce retry storms. we'll include sample backoff configs.
[07:50] Carlos Jimenez: next i'll outline the 48h synthetic surge test: 4 ramps (baseline, 4x, 8x, 12x peaks) with cohort skew scenarios: skew A-heavy, C-heavy, mixed. measure p50/p95/p99, token-savings delta, cache footprint, GC cycles, batch shape distribution.
[08:14] Priya Shah: timeframe for that test?
[08:16] Carlos Jimenez: we'll start as soon as we get the greenlight on VPC window and the cohorts from Priya — target to start by Monday 2026-11-29, run 48h, then analyze.
[08:26] Tom Nguyen: is Monday realistic? we need to confirm infra calendar, Danielle?
[08:30] Danielle Brooks: I can open the VPC peering tonight for a 72-hour window to be safe; will confirm in the action items.
[08:37] Maya Patel: perfect. any competitors or vendor constraints we should call out?
[08:41] Priya Shah: one of our infra folks mentioned a proof-of-concept with SageCloud that had poor session-affinity support; if we find affinity useful we'll call it out vs competitors.
[08:50] Carlos Jimenez: noted — we'll include a short section comparing behaviors.
[08:54] Maya Patel: ok wrapping up: recap of next steps and owners. Carlos to run the synthetic test and upload logs, Maya to send eviction-policy and example configs, Priya to share cohorts and metrics. Danielle to open VPC window. we'll meet next week for the deep dive.
[09:10] Priya Shah: thanks all, appreciate the clarity.
[09:14] Tom Nguyen: thanks, talk soon.
[09:16] Maya Patel: thank you, bye.
---

notes: Transcript includes realistic disfluencies, mis-heard words, and informal speech. Customer prioritized p99 stability over marginal token savings; agreed on conservative TTLs and session-affinity for interactive flows. Team to run a 48h surge test with cohort skews.
